2.add: Odor therefore acted on feeding motivation and the search for its source, whereas the electric field guided the final attack on the hidden fish.

3.add: Agar screening removed competing mechanical and visual cues while the sensory system of the predator stayed intact.

5.add: Direct current and a 1-Hz sinusoid both directed attacks to the active outlets, so the dipole field itself was the target.

6.add: The semi-natural setting preserved swimming behavior while the odor stimulation and the plate defined the encounter, so distance and trajectory could be compared between the two species.

7.add: The local field falls with distance from the dipole, so the same source current gives a weaker stimulus to a more distant shark.

8.add: The most frequent responses occurred within 5 cm in hammerheads and within 10 cm in sandbars, whereas the farthest responses were beyond 30 cm in both species.

9.add: Angle and distance together estimate the local field at the moment an orientation began.

10.add: The lowest measured responses came from the modeled field at orientation onset, and responses below 1 nV/cm show strong sensitivity of the whole sensory system.

11.add: The wide head therefore contributes to search coverage and to the geometry of turning toward a detected source.

12.add: Equal detection range can coexist with different interception performance, because trunk flexure and trajectory determine how a detected target is brought to the mouth.

13.add: The jelly-filled canal conducts the external voltage to the receptor epithelium, and dissociated receptor cells permit patch-clamp analysis of the channels that amplify it.

third_paragraph.14: The authors proposed that proton conduction may contribute to ampullary function. The measured proton conductivity indicates that the jelly can serve as a conductive path for voltage from the pore to the receptor epithelium.
third_paragraph.15: Chemical composition and electrical measurement together support a hydrated, sulfated matrix as the conductive medium of the canal. Membrane ion-channel amplification in the receptor cells provides a separate step in sensing the field.

16.add: The preparation preserves a tissue-level circuit, and single-cell recordings add channel-level evidence about the conductances that generate the response.

17.add: Tetrodotoxin separates sodium-dependent spikes from the preceding synaptic potential, so the recorded nerve response reflects the synaptic drive from the receptor epithelium.

18.add: Currents carried by calcium and potassium channels in single receptor cells are candidate sources of this activity.

19.add: Afferent output is therefore a temporally structured spike train that follows the polarity of the field as it alternates.

third_paragraph.20: Higher sensitivity at weak fields comes with earlier saturation, because an afferent can reach a saturated response before another neuron becomes strongly modulated. Population diversity could therefore support detection and intensity representation over different ranges, with sensitive afferents covering weak fields and less sensitive ones covering stronger fields.
third_paragraph.21: Saturation means that a response approaches a limit despite continued stimulus increase. It constrains what one afferent can report about source strength, while temporal information and the activity of afferents with other gains remain available.

22.add: The recordings connect receptor output to slow natural electrical fluctuations, with the most sensitive unit tuned near 1 Hz.

23.add: The physiological finding is the decline of the response during a maintained step, with a time constant of approximately 4 seconds, and adaptation emphasizes changes in the field over steady levels.

24.add: The slopes on the two sides of the optimum describe how steeply sensitivity falls for slower and faster fields.

third_paragraph.25: Localization of CaV1.3 and BK in receptor membranes, nuclear envelopes and kinocilia identifies candidate cellular sites for the channels that shape receptor activity. A nuclear-localization sequence tested through mutations in transfected cells was proposed to account for the nuclear signal.

26.add: Calcium entry can depolarize the receptor and drive release of transmitter onto the afferent.

27.add: Blockers of calcium entry and of BK channels each altered the current, so the dominant measured outward current of the receptor cell is BK mediated.

28.add: Agreement among current recordings, blocker responses, expression and cellular localization strengthens the assignment of CaV1.3 and BK to the electrosensory cells.

29.add: Heterologous expression isolates the molecular properties of the channel itself.

31.add: Neutralizing the charge weakened sensor-pore coupling, which links the positive charge of the motif to the efficient coupling that lowers the activation voltage.

32.add: Neutralizing the motif in skate CaV1.3 and inserting it into rat CaV1.3 produce opposite changes in activation, which together identify the charged residues as a determinant of low-voltage opening.

33.add: Skate BK channels therefore allow calcium-driven depolarization to build up before potassium feedback repolarizes the cell.

34.add: The reciprocal mutations moved conductance toward the species that supplied the substituted residues, which establishes a sequence-dependent contribution to pore function.

35.add: Startle tests checked that the reduced time near the active electrode was not a general impairment of mobility.

36.add: The shark outward current was voltage-gated and was inhibited by 4-AP, whereas the skate outward current depended on calcium and BK channels.

37.add: Accessory subunits or other cellular factors may account for the faster deactivation of native currents compared with cloned currents at some voltages.

38.add: Reduced voltage-sensor relaxation was proposed from kinetic evidence to account for the weak inactivation of the shark channel.

39.add: Nifedipine blocked the shark depolarization and 4-AP slowed repolarization, which identifies calcium entry and KV channels as the two components of the spike.

40.add: Both conductances remained available across repeated cycles.

third_paragraph.41: The assay measures membrane addition associated with exocytosis, so the capacitance increase reports the amount of vesicle fusion. Calcium entry triggers vesicle fusion in both shark and skate receptors, and the steps that follow fusion lead to transmitter action on the afferent.
third_paragraph.42: A larger readily releasable pool offers an explanation for the faster release saturation in shark cells, and free cytoplasmic vesicles may refill the pool as proposed from other ribbon synapses. Electron microscopy establishes synaptic architecture while capacitance and current recordings test its functional output.

43.add: The estimated tenfold difference in vesicle release per voltage event parallels the broader ventilation response of catsharks and the lower-frequency preference of skates.

44.add: Plasticity in this circuit was proposed to generate the cancellation signal, which cancels the input that is predictable from the ventilation cycle.

45.add: The recorded frequency shift is a direct experimental result, and tuning that matches the ventilation frequencies of conspecifics is a suggested ecological function.

inserts.title: An electric dipole has a source and a sink
paragraphs: An electric dipole consists of a current source and a nearby current sink. Current leaves the source, flows through the seawater and returns to the sink, so the field has a direction at every point around the pair. The dipole is a physical model of a small animal in seawater.

Kalmijn buried seawater-bridge outlets under sand and passed 4 µA between them, which approximates the strength of the electrical signal of a living plaice. Catsharks and rays dug at the active outlets and ignored identical outlets without current.
A dipole field is stronger near the outlets and weaker with distance. A predator that follows the field toward its strongest region reaches the outlets, which is the behavior seen in the experiment.
notes: A dipole is the simplest electrical model of a small animal in seawater.
Structure.
A dipole consists of a current source and a sink.
Current flows through the seawater from one to the other.
Strength of the model.
The buried outlets carried 4 microamperes, which approximates the signal of a living plaice.
Waveforms.
Either a 1-hertz sinusoidal current or direct current was used.
Both directed attacks to the active outlets.
Behavior.
After odor-induced arousal, catsharks and rays dug at the active outlets as though attacking prey.
Identical buried outlets without current did not elicit these responses.
Competition test.
A whiting piece placed 5 centimeters from the outlets supplied odor.
Directed attacks nevertheless favored the electrical source.
Field shape.
The field is strongest near the outlets and weakens with distance, so the animal can follow it to the source.
Why use artificial dipoles.
An artificial dipole separates the electrical field from every other property of a living fish.
If predators attack the outlets, the field alone is a sufficient cue.

inserts.title: Source current differs from local field strength
paragraphs: Source current is the current delivered through the outlets of a dipole, measured in microamperes. Field strength is the voltage gradient at the position of the animal, measured in microvolts per centimeter. The two quantities are related through the geometry of the dipole and the conductivity of seawater.

The apparatus delivered a constant 6.0 µA through outlets separated by 1 cm. The local field encountered by a shark depended on its distance from the dipole, on the angle of approach and on the properties of seawater.

A distant shark therefore experienced a weaker field from the same source current. Behavioral sensitivity is reported as the field at the position where an orientation began, which allows comparison with the thresholds of sensory cells.
notes: A source and the stimulus that it produces at a distance are different quantities.
Source current.
Current in microamperes describes what the apparatus delivers.
The experiment used a constant 6.0 microamperes.
Local field.
Field strength in microvolts per centimeter is the gradient at the position of the shark.
It is the stimulus that the receptors encounter.
Dependence on geometry.
The local field depends on distance, on the angle of approach and on seawater properties.
Stimulus control.
A battery-powered circuit and a series ammeter controlled and monitored the stimulus.
Four selectable dipoles allowed the target to be changed on the same plate.
Using the field.
Reporting the field at the start of a turn allows sensitivity to be compared across species and with sensory cells.
Controlling the apparatus.
Seawater-filled tubing separated the metal electrodes from the swimming animal, which reduced local chemical cues.
Both species bit the active dipole and ignored inactive dipoles.
Switching off the current.
Repeated biting stopped when the current was switched off, so the target position and the electrical activation could be manipulated independently.

inserts.title: Behavioral thresholds depend on a response criterion
paragraphs: A behavioral threshold is the stimulus level at which an animal reliably performs a defined response. It is set by the criterion that the observer chooses and by the motivation of the animal. Approximately 35 to 40 percent of orientations began below 0.01 µV/cm.
Kajiura and Holland defined orientation as a course change greater than 20° or a bite. Approximately 70% of orientations began below 0.1 µV/cm, and the most sensitive responses were below 1 nV/cm.

The threshold of a sensory cell is defined by its own response criterion, such as a change in membrane voltage or firing. Behavioral and cellular thresholds measure different things, so comparing them requires knowing how each was defined.
notes: A threshold is always defined by a criterion for what counts as a response.
Behavioral criterion.
An orientation was a course change greater than 20 degrees or a bite.
The estimated field at the onset of each orientation was the stimulus.
Distribution of responses.
Both species began approximately 70 percent of orientations below 0.1 microvolt per centimeter.
About 35 to 40 percent began below 0.01 microvolt per centimeter.
Most sensitive responses.
The lowest values were below 1 nanovolt per centimeter.
Cellular thresholds.
A sensory cell has its own criterion, such as a change in membrane voltage.
The two kinds of threshold are not interchangeable.
Dependence on motivation.
Feeding odor motivated the sharks to search, and the lowest responses depend on modeling of the source field.
Why criteria matter.
A stricter criterion gives a higher threshold and a looser one gives a lower threshold.
A threshold is therefore a property of the measurement as well as the animal.
Species comparison.
The distributions of the two species overlapped despite the difference in head shape.

inserts.title: Pores and canals connect skin to receptor cells
paragraphs: Each ampulla of Lorenzini opens to the skin through a pore and a jelly-filled canal. The canal conducts the voltage at the pore to a receptor epithelium at its inner end. The structure is organized so that a voltage at the pore reaches the receptor cells with little loss.

Bellono and colleagues stained the ventral canal network of the little skate with Alcian Blue. Isolated ampullae retained short canal segments and attached afferent nerves, and dissociated receptor cells were accessible to patch-clamp electrodes. Scale bars of 400 µm and 5 µm accompany the organ and cellular images.

The receptor cells convert voltage into activity and release neurotransmitter onto the afferent nerves. The pore, canal, receptor cells and nerve therefore form a chain from external voltage to a neural signal.
notes: The ampulla is a series of structures that carries a voltage from the skin to a nerve.
Pore and canal.
A skin pore opens into a jelly-filled canal.
The canal conducts the external voltage inward.
Receptor epithelium.
The receptor cells at the inner end convert the voltage into cellular activity.
Nerves.
Afferent nerves carry sensory signals toward the brain.
Receptor cells transmit to them through released neurotransmitters.
Preparations.
Alcian Blue revealed the ventral canal network.
Isolated ampullae kept short canal segments and nerves.
Scale bars of 400 micrometers and 5 micrometers accompany the published images.
Cellular access.
Dissociated receptor cells could be recorded with patch-clamp electrodes.
Why the structure helps.
The canal is filled with jelly that conducts the voltage between the pore and the receptor cells.
Separating the external opening from the receptors allows the receptors to sit deep in the skin.
Preparations used.
Whole-organ dissection kept the canal and nerve attachments.
Dissociated cells allowed control of voltage and recording of single-channel currents.

inserts.title: A salt bridge shunts the canal of an isolated ampulla
paragraphs: A shunt is a low-resistance path that carries current around part of a circuit. In the isolated ampulla, a salt bridge connected the canal side directly to the nerve side and held the transampullary voltage near its resting operating range. The preparation separates the receptor epithelium from the nerve that it drives.
Clusin and Bennett used separate saline compartments to deliver current and measure voltage across the receptor epithelium. Removing or restoring the shunt changed the electrical load on the organ.

The change in load separated spontaneous activity from output evoked by the stimulus. Epithelial current and the response of the nerve on the receiving side of the synapse could be monitored together. Spontaneous activity is the baseline against which stimulus-evoked changes are measured.
notes: A shunt makes it possible to control the voltage across the receptor epithelium.
Isolated organ.
Skate ampullae were isolated with their canals and afferent nerves attached.
Separate saline compartments held the canal and nerve sides.
Shunt.
A salt bridge shunted the canal.
This kept the transampullary voltage close to its resting operating range.
Stimulation.
Current delivered between compartments imposed small voltage stimuli without a freely swimming animal.
Monitoring.
Epithelial current and the response of the nerve on the receiving side of the synapse were recorded together.
Load.
Removing or restoring the shunt changed the electrical load, which helped separate spontaneous activity from stimulus-evoked output.
Questions answered by the preparation.
The recordings relate an external perturbation to current through the receptor epithelium.
The same recordings relate it to the response of the postsynaptic nerve.
Spontaneous activity.
The ampulla is active without a stimulus, so evoked responses are changes relative to that activity.

inserts.title: Tetrodotoxin isolates the synaptic potential
paragraphs: Tetrodotoxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, which generate action potentials in nerve cells. With spikes blocked, the slower synaptic potential that precedes them can be measured by itself. The postsynaptic nerve is the afferent ending that receives transmitter from the receptor cells.

Clusin and Bennett applied 0.1 µM tetrodotoxin to the shunted ampulla. A lumen-negative stimulus of 5 µV depolarized the postsynaptic nerve, and a lumen-positive stimulus of 10 µV hyperpolarized it. The tissue therefore transmitted changes much smaller than ordinary cellular voltage excursions.

The opposite signs show how the polarity of the stimulus changes the drive on the afferent. Small stimuli produced large changes in nerve potential without a comparably large change in total epithelial current. The sign of the stimulus determines whether the afferent is driven toward or away from threshold.
notes: Blocking spikes reveals the synaptic input that normally triggers them.
Tetrodotoxin.
It blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and abolishes action potentials.
The synaptic potential remains and can be recorded.
Polarity.
A lumen-negative stimulus of 5 microvolts depolarized the nerve.
A lumen-positive stimulus of 10 microvolts hyperpolarized it.
Terms.
Depolarization makes the membrane voltage less negative.
Hyperpolarization makes it more negative.
Size of the effect.
The stimuli were far smaller than ordinary cellular voltage excursions.
Total epithelial current changed little.
Meaning.
Opposite signs constrain how the receptor converts an environmental voltage into drive on the afferent.
Why the sign matters.
Depolarization of the nerve moves its voltage toward spike threshold, and hyperpolarization moves it away.
A receptor that responds with opposite signs to opposite polarities can encode the direction of a field.
Small stimuli.
The stimuli were a few microvolts, much smaller than ordinary cellular voltage excursions.
The organ therefore acts as a sensitive amplifier of weak voltages.

inserts.title: Period histograms align spikes to the stimulus cycle
paragraphs: A period histogram groups spikes by their position within one cycle of a repeating stimulus. Spikes that cluster at one phase produce a peak, and a reduction in spikes at another phase produces a trough.

Tricas and New applied a 1-Hz sinusoidal field to a stingray afferent with a regular resting spike train. As the peak-to-peak intensity increased from 0.05 to 0.26 µV/cm, firing rose during one phase and the neuron became silent during the opposite phase.

The histogram separates temporal locking from a change in overall spontaneous discharge. A neuron can signal the direction of the field through the phase at which it fires, even when its average rate is unchanged.
notes: A period histogram shows the timing of spikes relative to the stimulus.
Construction.
Each spike is assigned its position within one cycle of the stimulus.
Successive cycles are overlaid.
Resting activity.
The afferent fired a regular spike train in the absence of a stimulus.
Responses to the field.
A 1-hertz field increased firing during one phase.
At greater intensity it silenced the neuron during the opposite phase.
Intensity range.
Peak-to-peak field intensity increased from 0.05 to 0.26 microvolt per centimeter.
What the histogram reveals.
It distinguishes a change in the timing of firing from a change in overall spontaneous discharge.
Signal content.
The phase at which the neuron fires carries directional information about the field.
The neuron signals the sign of the field as well as its presence.
Preparation.
Round stingrays were immobilized, and artificial ventilation maintained respiration while uniform fields were applied across the body.
Spike counts across a cycle.
Each histogram shows spike counts across one stimulus cycle for a different field intensity.
The change from a gentle modulation to a deep trough follows the increase in intensity.

inserts.title: Gain describes sensitivity to changes in intensity
paragraphs: Gain is the change in neural response per unit change in stimulus intensity. A high-gain neuron changes its firing steeply for a small change in field, and a low-gain neuron needs a larger change to produce the same effect. The slope is the quantity that describes gain at each stimulus level.

Tricas and New calculated local slopes of rate-intensity curves across successive stimulus intervals. The most sensitive example kept a steep response over the weakest range and then lost incremental gain.

Gain therefore varies with the stimulus level at which it is measured. Neurons with different gains cover different ranges of intensity, so a population of afferents can represent weak and strong fields. Gain also depends on whether the stimulus is weak or strong, so a single number does not describe a neuron.
notes: Sensitivity depends on where on the intensity axis a neuron is measured.
Definition.
Gain describes how strongly the response changes for a change in stimulus intensity.
Local slope.
Slopes were calculated across successive stimulus intervals of each rate-intensity curve.
High-gain example.
The most sensitive afferent had a steep response only over the weakest range.
It then lost incremental gain as intensity increased.
Lower-gain afferents.
Lower-gain units declined over different operating ranges.
Population.
Different units operate over different ranges, so together they can represent a wide range of field strengths.
Question addressed.
The measurements ask how a single afferent changes its firing as the field becomes stronger.
The answer depends on the range of intensities tested.
Interpreting the curves.
A steep part of a rate-intensity curve means that small changes in intensity change firing.
A flat part means that the neuron no longer distinguishes stronger fields.
Resting and peak rates.
Peak firing and resting firing were both measured as the field increased.
The difference between them describes how much the response can be modulated.
Variation among units.
Different afferents had markedly different rate-intensity relationships in the same preparation.

inserts.title: Adaptation emphasizes changes over steady fields
paragraphs: Adaptation is a decline in response during a maintained stimulus. The response is largest when the stimulus changes and smaller when the stimulus stays constant. Repeating steps allowed the response time course to be averaged across presentations.

Tricas and New applied direct-current field steps lasting 60 s to round-stingray afferents. A 2.2-µV/cm step caused a large initial rise in spike rate, followed by a return toward the resting rate with a time constant of approximately 4 s.

A swimming shark moves its pores through the field of a stationary prey source, so the input at the receptors changes with time. Adaptation therefore favors the changes that carry information about a source while a steady background is discounted.
notes: A system that adapts reports changes, and a changing input is what a moving predator experiences.
Definition.
Adaptation is a decline of response during maintained stimulation.
Step stimulus.
Direct-current field steps lasted 60 seconds.
A 2.2-microvolt-per-centimeter step produced a large initial increase in spike rate.
Time course.
The rate returned toward the resting rate with a time constant of approximately 4 seconds.
Repeated steps allowed averaging of the response.
Meaning for the animal.
Swimming changes the field sampled at the pores, so a stationary prey source produces a changing input.
Distinction.
The physical input is maintained while the afferent output is transient.
Why the decay matters.
A decay time constant of about 4 seconds means that the response falls substantially within a few seconds of a step.
Slow changes in the field are therefore reported less than fast changes.
Sampling by swimming.
As the shark swims past a source, the field at its pores changes continuously, which keeps the afferents responding.

inserts.title: A window current sustains activity near rest
paragraphs: A window current is a persistent current that flows where the activation curve of a channel overlaps the curve of its availability. Over that voltage range, channels open and remain available at the same time.

Bellono and colleagues patch-clamped dissociated little-skate receptor cells with cesium inside to suppress potassium currents. The native calcium conductance reached half-maximal activation near −52 mV, and the window current extended from about −70 to −30 mV and peaked near −58 mV.

The peak lies close to the normal operating voltage of the receptor. A calcium current that is active at rest allows small changes in membrane voltage to change calcium entry and therefore transmitter release.
notes: A window current allows a channel to contribute at voltages near rest.
Definition.
A window current flows where activation and availability overlap.
Channels in that range are open and not inactivated.
Recording method.
Voltage clamp holds the membrane at commanded voltages while measuring current.
Cesium inside the cell suppressed potassium currents.
Numbers.
Half-maximal activation was near minus 52 millivolts.
The window extended from about minus 70 to minus 30 millivolts and peaked near minus 58 millivolts.
Receptor operating voltage.
The peak lies close to the normal operating voltage of the receptor.
Consequence.
Small voltage changes near rest change calcium entry, which controls release at the synapse.
Pharmacology.
L-type calcium-channel modulators altered the current.
Tested sodium-channel antagonists and several other calcium-channel antagonists did not.
Molecular identity.
Transcript measurements implicated CaV1.3, an L-type channel.
Reading the current.
An inward current carries positive charge into the cell and depolarizes it.
Activation at unusually negative voltages means the channel opens close to rest.
Inactivation.
Inactivation reduces the number of channels available during sustained stimulation, and its slow development leaves the window current.

inserts.title: Negative feedback returns the membrane toward rest
paragraphs: Negative feedback is a process in which a change sets in motion an opposing change. In the receptor cell, calcium entry depolarizes the membrane, and the resulting rise in calcium recruits an outward potassium current that opposes the depolarization. The same feedback also sets how quickly the cell can respond to the next change in voltage.

Bellono and colleagues measured outward currents with a potassium-based solution. Tetraethylammonium, iberiotoxin and charybdotoxin reduced the current, calcium-channel inhibition also reduced it, and enhancing calcium entry increased it.

The linked effects of these manipulations indicate coupling between the inward calcium current and BK-mediated outward current. Potassium efflux returns the membrane toward negative voltages and sets the timing of the next depolarization. Each of these steps was tested with a drug or an ion substitution.
notes: The receptor cell contains its own mechanism for limiting depolarization.
Sequence.
Depolarization opens calcium channels.
Calcium recruits BK channels, and potassium efflux repolarizes the membrane.
Measurement.
A potassium-based solution allowed the outward currents to be measured.
Blockers.
Tetraethylammonium, iberiotoxin and charybdotoxin reduced the current.
Iberiotoxin and charybdotoxin are selective BK antagonists.
Calcium dependence.
Calcium-channel inhibition reduced the current.
Enhancing calcium entry increased it.
Meaning.
The coupling supplies negative feedback that shapes the oscillations of the receptor.
Why two features matter.
A calcium current alone would depolarize the cell until calcium entry stopped.
A potassium current activated by calcium returns the membrane toward rest.
Evidence from perturbation.
Changing the calcium current changed the potassium current in the same direction.
This linked effect supports functional coupling between the two currents.
Solutions.
Replacing the cesium-based solution with a potassium-based solution allowed outward currents to be measured.
Cesium had suppressed potassium currents in the earlier recordings.
Role in the cell.
Potassium efflux counteracts depolarization from calcium entry, so the membrane voltage can oscillate.

inserts.title: Gating charge and tail current report channel coupling
paragraphs: Gating current records the movement of charge inside the voltage-sensing parts of a channel. Ionic conductance records current through the open pore, and the relation between the two reports how efficiently sensor movement opens the pore. Both records are obtained from the same cell under voltage clamp.

Bellono and colleagues measured both in cells expressing skate or rat CaV1.3. Voltage-dependent charge movement was broadly similar, but skate channels reached substantial conductance with less relative sensor movement.

A tail current is the current recorded after the voltage returns to a negative value, and it reports channels that were open at the end of the command. Skate channels produced larger tail currents for comparable gating charge, which indicates enhanced coupling.
notes: Two measurements separate sensor movement from pore opening.
Gating current.
Gating current records charge movement within the voltage sensors.
It does not record ion flow through the open pore.
Conductance.
Ionic conductance records current through the open channel.
Result.
Charge movement was broadly similar in skate and rat channels.
Skate channels reached substantial conductance with less relative sensor movement.
Tail current.
The voltage returned to minus 100 millivolts after a depolarizing command.
The tail current reports the channels that were open.
Meaning.
A low activation voltage reflects enhanced coupling between sensor and pore and not a larger number of moving charges.
Skate and rat comparison.
Skate and rat CaV1.3 were expressed under matched recording conditions.
Differences between them therefore belong to the channels.
Interpretation.
Efficient coupling means that a given movement of the voltage sensor opens more of the pore, which lowers the voltage required for activation.
Voltage sensors and pore.
A voltage-gated channel contains voltage-sensitive elements coupled to an ion-conducting pore.
Coupling describes how well sensor movement opens the pore.
Return to negative voltage.
Returning from a depolarizing command to minus 100 millivolts produced larger skate tail currents for comparable gating charge.

inserts.title: Capacitance increases when vesicles fuse
paragraphs: Membrane capacitance is the ability of the membrane to store charge, and it increases with surface area. When a synaptic vesicle fuses with the cell surface, its membrane adds to the surface and capacitance rises. Capacitance is measured in the same cell that supplies the calcium current, so release and calcium entry can be compared directly.

Bellono and colleagues gave a 200-ms pulse to −20 mV, which elicited calcium current and a capacitance increase in both shark and skate receptors. Cadmium blocked the inward current and the capacitance change.

Longer pulses produced larger responses, but shark responses approached saturation more rapidly while skate capacitance increased more steadily. Capacitance therefore provides a readout of release that differs between the two receptor types. Skate cells release transmitter more gradually, and shark cells reach saturation sooner.
notes: Capacitance gives a way to follow exocytosis in a single cell.
Principle.
Capacitance reflects membrane surface area.
Vesicle fusion adds membrane and increases capacitance.
Stimulus.
A 200-millisecond pulse to minus 20 millivolts elicited calcium current in both species.
Calcium dependence.
Cadmium blocked the inward current and the capacitance change.
Duration.
Longer pulses produced larger release-associated responses.
Shark responses approached saturation more rapidly than skate responses.
Controls.
Membrane-conductance controls limited recording artifacts that could mimic capacitance changes.
Controls for artifacts.
Membrane-conductance controls limited recording artifacts that could mimic capacitance changes.
Cadmium blocked both calcium current and capacitance change.
Species difference.
Shark cells approached saturation of release sooner than skate cells.
Skate capacitance increased more steadily with pulse duration.
Calcium and release.
Release from receptor cells depends on calcium entry, as the cadmium experiment shows.
The link supports a role for the calcium channel in driving the afferent.
Readout limits.
Capacitance measures membrane addition from vesicle fusion.
It does not count transmitter molecules or postsynaptic receptor openings.

inserts.title: Reafference is self-generated sensory input
paragraphs: Reafference is sensory stimulation caused by an animal's own movement. For an electrosensory fish, breathing movements of the gills generate electrical signals at the skin that are predictable in time. The dorsal octavolateralis nucleus receives input from the electrosensory afferents.

Montgomery and Bodznick recorded ascending efferent neurons in the dorsal octavolateralis nucleus of the little skate while ventilation timing was measured near the gills. A 2-µV dipole stimulus coupled to ventilation produced responses that declined over minutes. Neurons were recorded in the little skate under controlled conditions.

After 10 minutes of coupling, the mean reduction in responsive neurons was 44.3%, and turning the stimulus off revealed an opposite-sign cancellation response at the trained respiratory phase. The circuit learns the predictable input and subtracts it.
notes: A weak external signal can only be detected if the animal's own signal is removed.
Definition.
Reafference is sensory stimulation caused by the movement of the animal itself.
Source in the skate.
Ventilation moves the gills and produces predictable electrical input at the skin.
Recording site.
Ascending efferent neurons in the dorsal octavolateralis nucleus were recorded.
This nucleus is the first medullary electrosensory processing nucleus.
Training.
A 2-microvolt dipole stimulus was coupled to ventilation.
Responses declined over minutes, and uncoupled presentations still evoked responses.
Cancellation.
After 10 minutes the mean reduction in responsive neurons was 44.3 percent.
Turning the stimulus off revealed an opposite-sign response at the trained phase.
Controls.
Uncoupled presentations of the stimulus still evoked responses, so the decline depended on pairing with ventilation and not on fatigue.
Circuit.
Primary afferents contact basal dendrites, while cerebellar parallel fibers and inhibitory interneurons contact apical dendrites.
Plasticity in this circuit was proposed to generate the cancellation signal.
